_readme: A bootstrap run of `src/tools/configure.py` — the answers for one person, in the shape that tool documents.
EVERY VALUE IS INVENTED FOR THE TEST. The person is the one this repository's other fixtures already use
when a differently-shaped applicant is needed (`src/pipeline/test_build_cover_letter.py`,
`src/forms/test_draft_form_spec.py`): a registered nurse in Toronto with a B.Sc.N. and a diploma and no
master's, and no LinkedIn — deliberately NOT the example's shape, because a bootstrap test that starts
from a US-resident master's holder with a LinkedIn profile proves nothing about the example's own values
being replaced. The e-mail is on `example.org`, which can never reach anyone.
The keys are paths relative to the data directory; the values merge INTO the shipped example. Objects
merge key by key, lists and scalars replace, and `null` DELETES the key — which is how the example's
`legal_name_native`, `platform_experience` and `ead_expiry` are removed rather than answered with
something plausible. `src/tools/configure.py` refuses to write any file that is not still its example.
WHY THE WORK-AUTHORISATION ANSWERS ARE WHAT THEY ARE: the drafter answers a generic 'are you authorised
to work' question from `standard_answers.us_work_authorized` and a citizenship question from
`candidate.citizenship`. This person is a US citizen by birth who lives in Canada as a permanent
resident, so `Yes` is the truthful answer on either reading, and `work_authorization: us_citizen` is what
the screening reads where the value decides which US work-authorisation requirements are a bar.

resume.summary: I am a registered nurse in Toronto with nine years of acute care behind me, six of them in a downtown emergency department, and I am looking for the next unit where the hard part is the handoff rather than the assessment. I triage walk-in and ambulance arrivals, start and titrate IV therapy, and read telemetry well enough to know when to escalate before the numbers say so. I have precepted six new graduate nurses through their first year and signed off their initial triage decisions, which is where I learned that a checklist only works when the person beside you can say out loud what they are unsure about. What I would bring is the habit of writing a handoff the next nurse can act on.

I assess and prioritise walk-in and ambulance arrivals, start and titrate IV therapy, and hand patients over to the inpatient teams who take them next, and I have precepted six new graduate nurses through their first year on the unit. What I would bring here is the handoff discipline that comes from a department that never really empties: a written record the next nurse can act on, an independent double-check on high-alert medications, and a habit of naming what has not yet been checked.
